newsitem.title: UK: UK windfall tax to raise 5.0 bln pounds - paper.
newsitem.headline: UK windfall tax to raise 5.0 bln pounds - paper.

text.p: The proposed windfall tax on privatised British companies will raise a minimum of 5.0 billion pounds ($8.3 billion), when it is unveiled at next week's budget, the Financial Times said on Friday.
The paper said it would yield the Labour government a minimum of 2.0 billion pounds more than it has set-out to pay for its "welfare-to-work" programme.
It said British Telecommunications Plc was preparing to make the biggest individual payment, which executives estimate at up to a billion pounds.

And senior government members said Chancellor Gordon Brown, who will reveal his first budget next Wednesday, was resisting pressure to drop the planned abolition of the 20 percent tax credit on dividends, the FT added.

The paper said Brown would announce the total yield from the windfall tax on profits but not the liabilities of individual companies, sticking to the convention that a firm's tax bill is a private issue for it and the Inland Revenue.
But he will avoid creating stock market uncertainty by announcing a much simpler formula for calculating each firm's liability than was expected.
"It will be very easy for you to work out who pays what," the paper quoted a senior government figure as saying. "Each company's payment will be based on published and readily available information."

The FT said the companies to be hit would be the regional electricity firms, the two main electricity generating companies, the water companies, British Telecom, the British Gas spin-off firms, Railtrack Plc and BAA Plc.

It said Brown's budget was also likely to to include a start on on his aim of establishing a new 10 pence bottom rate of income tax and changing so-called benefit tapers to reduce loss of social security payments to individuals who take low earning employment.
The Independent newspaper said Brown would signal a long-term overhaul of the tax and benefit systems as well as radical plans to reshape the entire budget process.

As well as the measures on benefits and reducing the burden on the low-paid, Brown will also emphasise the use of the tax system to cut pollution and encourage energy conservation, the Independent said.
It said Brown had met the Deputy Prime Minister John Prescott on Thursday to discuss "green taxes", which would form a key part of the budget. REUTER AS ($ = 0.600 British Pounds)
